title: The Dark Side of Steam
summary: Steam made cloth cheap and cities rich, but it also had a dark side. Children worked long hours in noisy mills and deep, dangerous coal mines, boilers sometimes exploded, and smoke turned the sky grey. Brave people spoke up, and slowly new laws made work safer and fairer.

sections.heading: Small Hands in the Roaring Mill
paragraphs: Imagine it is five o'clock on a dark winter morning in a Lancashire town in about 1830. A factory bell clangs. Hundreds of people hurry through the wet streets, and among them are children, some only eight or nine years old, rubbing their eyes. Inside the mill the great steam engine is already hissing in its engine house. When the engineer opens the valve, the long line shafts overhead begin to turn, the leather belts slap into motion, and every spinning machine in the building wakes up at once. From that moment until the engine stops in the evening, the machines set the pace, and the people have to keep up.

Children had always worked. On farms and in cottage workshops they had fed chickens, carded wool and minded babies. But the mill was different. The steam engine did not get tired, and the owners who had paid a lot of money for it wanted it running for as many hours as possible. Twelve, thirteen or even more hours a day were common in the early 1800s, often with only short breaks to eat.

Why children? Partly because they were cheap: a child might earn a small fraction of a man's wage. Partly because their small bodies and nimble fingers suited certain jobs. A 'piecer' walked up and down beside the spinning mules, quickly twisting together threads that had snapped. A 'scavenger' crawled underneath the moving machinery to sweep up fluff and cotton waste, while the heavy carriage of the mule rolled back and forth just above them. Accidents happened. Hair, sleeves and fingers could be caught by unguarded gears, belts and shafts.

The air itself was a problem. Cotton spinning works best in warm, damp air, so many mills were kept hot and humid. Tiny fibres floated everywhere and were breathed in day after day. The noise of hundreds of machines was so loud that workers learned to talk by lip-reading. Long hours of standing could leave growing bodies bent or injured, and doctors at the time wrote about children with deformed legs.

Some of the earliest mill children were 'parish apprentices': orphans or children from very poor families who were sent by local officials to work in distant water-powered mills, often living in a dormitory beside the factory. As steam let mills move into towns, owners could more easily hire children who lived at home with their parents. For a poor family, a child's wage could mean the difference between eating and going hungry, which is one reason many parents felt they had no choice.

Not everyone accepted this. In 1830 a Yorkshire land agent named Richard Oastler wrote a furious open letter to a Leeds newspaper about children working in factories near Bradford. He argued that they were treated worse than enslaved people on sugar plantations, a shocking comparison at a time when Britain was arguing about ending slavery in its colonies. In 1832 a Member of Parliament, Michael Sadler, led a committee that collected evidence from mill workers, some of whom described being beaten to keep them awake at the end of long shifts. Later investigators thought some of the most dramatic stories in Sadler's report were exaggerated, but the report shocked the public and helped push Parliament to act.

sections.heading: The Factory Act of 1833
paragraphs: Parliament had already tried to protect mill children. A law of 1802, the Health and Morals of Apprentices Act, limited parish apprentices to 12 hours a day and banned them from working at night. A law of 1819 banned children under 9 from cotton mills. But these early laws had a fatal weakness: almost nobody checked whether they were obeyed. Local magistrates, who were sometimes friends or relatives of the mill owners, were supposed to enforce them, and they rarely did.

The Factory Act of 1833 was different, and it is often seen as a turning point. It applied to textile mills across the United Kingdom, not just cotton mills. Its main rules were simple enough to fit on a poster. Children under 9 could not be employed in most textile mills (silk mills were an exception). Children aged 9 to 13 were limited to 9 hours a day, and no more than 48 hours a week for the younger ones. Young people aged 13 to 18 could work no more than 12 hours a day. Nobody under 18 was allowed to work at night.

The Act also tried to make sure working children learned something. Children aged 9 to 13 were supposed to get two hours of schooling every day, and the mill had to keep a certificate from a schoolmaster to prove it. In practice the 'schools' were sometimes just a corner of the mill with a teacher who could barely read, and the inspectors themselves later called these education rules nearly impossible to carry out properly. Still, it was the start of an important idea: that children's time belonged partly to learning, not only to work.

The most important new idea was the inspector. The 1833 Act created a small team of government factory inspectors, paid by the state and reporting to the Home Office. They had the right to walk into mills, look at records and bring cases against owners who broke the law. At first there were only four inspectors for roughly 4,000 factories, so each one had an enormous area to cover. Clever owners also found ways around the rules. One trick was the 'relay system', where children worked in shifts so that the adults, and the steam engine, could keep going for 15 hours a day.

Even so, the inspectors' reports gave Parliament real information, year after year, and further laws followed. The Factory Act of 1844 required dangerous parts such as flywheels and gearing to be fenced in, stopped children and women from cleaning machinery while it was moving, and said accidents had to be reported. The Ten Hours Act of 1847, pushed for years by campaigners such as Lord Ashley (later the Earl of Shaftesbury) inside Parliament, Oastler outside it, and the mill owner John Fielden, cut the working day of women and young people in textile mills to about ten hours. Change was slow and uneven, but the direction was clear: the power of steam would have to be matched by rules that protected the people working beside it.

sections.heading: Darkness Under the Ground
paragraphs: Every steam engine had a hungry firebox, and that firebox needed coal. As engines spread through mills, ironworks, ships and railways, Britain dug more and more coal, and the mines went deeper. The steam engine and the coal mine were tied together in a loop: engines pumped water out of the pits, and the pits fed coal to the engines. But the people doing the digging paid a heavy price.

Picture a coal mine in Yorkshire around 1840. You climb into a basket or cage and are lowered down a shaft hundreds of feet into blackness. At the bottom, narrow tunnels stretch away, some so low that an adult cannot stand up. The only light comes from candles or small lamps. Somewhere ahead, men called hewers are cutting coal with picks. Behind them, the coal has to be moved to the bottom of the shaft, and much of that moving was done by women and children.

The youngest children, sometimes only five or six years old, were 'trappers'. Their job was to sit alone in the dark beside a wooden door and pull it open whenever a coal tub came through, then shut it again. These doors controlled the flow of fresh air through the mine, which was vital for keeping dangerous gases away. A trapper might sit there for twelve hours, mostly in darkness and silence. Older children and women worked as 'hurriers' or 'drawers', pushing or pulling heavy tubs of coal along tunnels too low to stand in, sometimes with a chain running from a belt around the waist.

Mines were dangerous in many ways. Roofs could collapse. Workers could fall down shafts or be crushed by tubs. Water could flood in. Worst of all were explosions. Coal seams can give off methane, a gas miners called 'firedamp'. If enough of it built up and met a naked flame, the result could be a blast that tore through the tunnels, followed by 'afterdamp', a choking mixture of gases left behind. Safety lamps, such as the one designed by Humphry Davy in 1815, helped, but explosions continued throughout the 1800s.

In July 1838, a sudden thunderstorm near Barnsley in Yorkshire caused a stream to overflow into the Huskar Colliery at Silkstone. Water poured into a passage where children were trying to escape. Twenty-six children died: 11 girls aged 8 to 16 and 15 boys aged 9 to 12. The disaster was reported to the young Queen Victoria, and it helped lead to a national investigation.

That investigation, the Children's Employment Commission, sent commissioners into mining districts to interview workers, and its report came out in May 1842. It was full of the miners' own words, and it included drawings, many by the artist Margaret Gillies, showing children crawling through tiny tunnels and dragging coal tubs. Many readers in comfortable homes had simply never imagined such scenes. Lord Ashley led the campaign in Parliament, and in 1842 the Mines and Collieries Act was passed. It banned all women and girls from working underground, and it banned boys under 10. Some mine owners fought hard to weaken the law, and enforcement took time, but it was another step: the coal that fed the steam age would no longer be dug by small children.

sections.heading: When Boilers Burst
paragraphs: A boiler is a strong metal container full of hot water and steam under pressure. As long as the metal holds and the pressure stays within safe limits, all that stored energy flows calmly into the engine. But if the boiler fails, the energy is released in an instant. The water inside is hotter than its normal boiling point, so when the pressure suddenly drops, much of it flashes into steam all at once and expands enormously. A boiler explosion could throw heavy metal plates hundreds of feet and wreck a whole building.

Why did boilers burst? Engineers who studied the wreckage found several common causes. Sometimes the water level fell too low, so the fire heated bare metal until it weakened. Sometimes a safety valve, which is meant to let out steam when the pressure gets too high, was stuck, badly adjusted or even deliberately tied down by an operator who wanted more power. Sometimes the boiler had been badly made, with weak joints or thin plates. And very often the metal had simply rusted and thinned over years of use. Inspection records from the late 1800s and early 1900s suggest corrosion was the most frequent cause of all.

The worst boiler disaster in American history happened on the Mississippi River. The Sultana was a large wooden side-wheel steamboat with four boilers, built in 1863 and designed to carry a few hundred passengers. In April 1865, the American Civil War was just ending, and thousands of Union soldiers who had survived terrible prison camps, such as Cahaba in Alabama and Andersonville in Georgia, were waiting near Vicksburg, Mississippi, to go home. Through a mix of haste and corruption, around 2,100 people were crammed aboard, most of them these weakened soldiers. One of the boilers had a leak, and instead of a proper repair that would have taken days, it was quickly patched.

At about two o'clock in the morning on 27 April 1865, a few miles north of Memphis, Tennessee, the boilers exploded. The blast tore through the crowded decks, and fire spread through the wooden boat. Many people who survived the explosion were thrown into the cold, fast-flowing river, swollen by spring floods. Other steamboats hurried to help, but the number of dead was enormous: the most recent estimate is about 1,164 people, and older counts go higher. More people died than in many famous shipwrecks, yet the news was overshadowed at the time by the end of the war and the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln less than two weeks earlier. Investigators blamed the faulty repair, low water in the boilers and the dangerous overloading.

Disasters on land happened too. In the 1860s, nearly 500 boiler explosions were recorded in Britain, killing over 700 people. In March 1905, a boiler explosion at the Grover Shoe Factory in Brockton, Massachusetts, killed 58 people and injured about 150, and the building collapsed and burned.

Out of these tragedies came something we now take for granted: safety inspection. In 1854, engineers and mill owners met in Manchester, including the famous engineer William Fairbairn, and formed what became the Manchester Steam Users' Association, officially founded in 1855. Its idea was simple: trained engineers would visit members' boilers regularly and look for danger signs before an accident happened. The inspections also helped save fuel. In the United States, the Hartford Steam Boiler Inspection and Insurance Company was founded in 1866, combining inspection with insurance. The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, formed in 1880 partly because of worries about boiler safety, published its Boiler Code in 1915. Rules like these, about thickness of metal, safety valves, testing and regular checks, are the ancestors of the safety codes that still protect every boiler and pressure vessel today.

sections.heading: Smoke, Soot and Stinking Rivers
paragraphs: Stand on a hill above Manchester in the 1840s and look down. Instead of a clear view you would see a grey-brown haze, pierced by hundreds of tall factory chimneys, each pouring out coal smoke. Soot settled on window sills, washing hung out to dry, buildings, trees and people's lungs. Visitors wrote about the sun looking pale and red through the smoke. Many towns had a distinctive smell of coal fires, and rain could fall dirty.

Coal smoke contains tiny particles of soot along with gases such as sulphur dioxide. Breathed in day after day, it made lung diseases more common, especially in crowded neighbourhoods close to the factories. The sulphur in the smoke could also mix with moisture in the air to make acid, which ate away at stone buildings and harmed plants.

Rivers suffered as well. Factories, dye works, tanneries and slaughterhouses dumped waste into them, and many towns let their sewage flow straight into the nearest river. In London, the Thames became so foul that in the hot summer of 1858 the smell was nicknamed the 'Great Stink'. Curtains in the Houses of Parliament, beside the river, were soaked in chemicals to try to block the smell. Cholera, a deadly disease spread by contaminated water, struck London several times in the 1830s, 1840s and 1850s. In response, the engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a huge new system of sewers between 1859 and 1875, and it used powerful steam engines in pumping stations to move the sewage away. So steam was part of the problem and part of the solution.

One of the most famous descriptions of life in a steam-age city was written by a young German named Friedrich Engels. His father owned textile businesses, and Engels was sent to work in a cotton firm in Manchester in 1842. He spent his spare time walking through the poorest districts and talking to workers. In 1845, at the age of 24, he published a book in German called The Condition of the Working Class in England. He described damp, overcrowded houses, filthy courtyards, polluted streams and families crammed into cellars, and he compared death rates in industrial cities with those in the rest of the country. His book has a strong political point of view, and historians read it alongside other evidence, but it gives a vivid picture of how hard life could be in the world's first great industrial city.

Slowly, laws began to tackle pollution too. The Alkali Act of 1863 targeted chemical works that released clouds of acid gas, and it created inspectors to check them. Laws against factory smoke followed, though they were weak for a long time. The worst air pollution disasters came even later: in December 1952, a thick smog in London, made mainly by coal smoke from homes, power stations and factories, caused thousands of deaths and led to the Clean Air Act of 1956. The smoky skies of the steam age took more than a century to clear.

sections.heading: Breaking Frames, Building Unions
paragraphs: Workers did not simply accept everything the new machines brought. The most famous protesters were the Luddites. Their movement began in March 1811 in Arnold, near Nottingham, and spread over the next few years to Yorkshire and Lancashire. They took their name from 'Ned Ludd' or 'General Ludd', a legendary figure who may never have existed, and some of their letters were signed in his name.

It is easy to think the Luddites were smashing steam engines, but that is not really what happened. In the Midlands, most of the machines they broke were stocking frames, hand-operated knitting machines used to make stockings and lace, especially 'wide frames' that produced cheap, poor-quality goods. In Yorkshire, skilled cloth finishers called croppers attacked shearing frames, machines that did their job faster and cheaper. In Lancashire, some protests targeted mills with power looms. The Luddites were not against all machines; they were angry about employers who used new machinery and new methods to cut wages, hire unskilled workers and destroy skilled trades, at a time of war, high food prices and real hunger.

The government's response was harsh. About 12,000 soldiers were sent to the troubled areas. In 1812 Parliament made breaking machines a crime that could be punished by death. One of the few people to speak up for the frame-breakers in Parliament was the young poet Lord Byron. In April 1812, Luddites attacked Rawfolds Mill in Yorkshire and were driven off with gunfire. Later that month, a mill owner named William Horsfall was shot and killed. After trials at York in January 1813, a number of men were hanged and others were sent to the prison colonies in Australia. By about 1816 the movement had faded.

A longer-lasting way for workers to push back was to join together. For many years, laws called the Combination Acts, passed in 1799 and 1800, made it illegal for workers to organise to demand better wages. After those laws were repealed in 1824, trade unions grew, though they were still often treated with suspicion. In 1834, six farm labourers from the village of Tolpuddle in Dorset were sentenced to be transported to Australia for swearing an oath when forming a union. Huge public protests followed, and they were pardoned and allowed to return. Their story became a symbol for the labour movement. Over the rest of the 1800s, unions, campaigners and reformers won shorter hours, safer conditions and, eventually, the right of more working men and then women to vote.

sections.heading: Cotton, Slavery and Empire
paragraphs: The steam-powered cotton mills of Lancashire had a hidden connection to a much darker story far away. Cotton does not grow in Britain's cool climate. Most of it had to be imported, and by the middle of the 1800s most came from the southern United States, where it was grown and picked by enslaved African Americans.

In 1793, Eli Whitney designed a cotton gin, a machine that quickly separated cotton fibres from their sticky seeds, a job that had been very slow by hand. Combined with the hungry demand from British and American mills, the gin made growing cotton hugely profitable across the American South. Instead of reducing the need for labour, it increased it, because cotton still had to be planted, hoed and picked by hand. The number of enslaved people in the United States grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to about 3.2 million in 1850. American cotton production rose from 750,000 bales in 1830 to 2.85 million bales in 1850.

In 1860, about 80 percent of the raw cotton arriving in Britain came from America. That meant the steam engines of Manchester, the wages of hundreds of thousands of mill workers and the profits of merchants in Liverpool were all bound up with slavery, even though slavery itself had been abolished in most of the British Empire in 1833. When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, the supply of cotton was cut off, and the Lancashire Cotton Famine left many mill workers unemployed and hungry. Remarkably, at a meeting in Manchester's Free Trade Hall on 31 December 1862, workers voted to support the Union side and its fight against slavery, even though it was costing them their jobs. President Abraham Lincoln wrote back in January 1863 to thank them.

Steam power also changed the balance of power between countries. Britain's cheap, machine-made cloth flooded markets around the world, including India, which had been famous for its fine hand-woven cotton for centuries. Steamships and, later, steam railways helped European empires move soldiers, goods and officials far more quickly, making it easier to control distant colonies and to ship their raw materials home. Historians still argue about how much empire contributed to Britain's industrial success, but it is clear that the benefits of the steam age were not shared fairly. Some people grew very rich, while many others, in Britain and around the world, carried much of the cost.

sections.heading: The Longest Shadow
paragraphs: There is one more cost of steam that nobody in the 1800s could see. When coal burns, the carbon in it combines with oxygen from the air to make carbon dioxide, an invisible gas. Every steam engine, every factory chimney and every coal fire released it into the air. For most of human history, scientists now know, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere had stayed at about 280 parts per million for thousands of years. Once people began burning coal on a huge scale, that number started to climb, and later the burning of oil and gas made it rise even faster.

A few scientists in the 1800s began to wonder about this. In 1896 the Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius published calculations suggesting that more carbon dioxide in the air would warm the Earth's surface. At the time, it seemed like a distant, almost curious idea. Today the concentration is well over 400 parts per million, more than half as much again as before the Industrial Revolution, and it is the main cause of the climate change the world is now trying to slow down. We will look at that story, and at what it means for the future of steam, in Part 19.

None of this means the steam engine was simply bad. It made goods cheaper, created new jobs, powered printing presses that spread knowledge, and eventually helped raise living standards for billions of people. But an honest history has to look at both sides: the brilliant engineering and the children in the mines, the cheap cloth and the cotton fields, the bright future and the smoky sky. The reformers who wrote reports, passed laws and inspected boilers were part of the steam story too.

And there was one more group of people asking hard questions. Engineers had spent more than a century improving engines by trial and error, saving a little coal here and a little there. Now some began to ask a bigger question: how good could a steam engine ever possibly get? Was there a limit? The search for the answer would lead to a completely new science.

deepDive: Historians have argued for a long time about how much the early Industrial Revolution helped or harmed ordinary workers, a debate often called the 'standard of living debate'. 'Optimists' point to rising real wages after about 1820, cheaper clothing and food, and growing populations. 'Pessimists' point to long hours, child labour, crowded and unhealthy cities, and the loss of skilled trades. Recent research using records of people's heights (a sign of childhood nutrition and health) and death rates suggests that living conditions for many workers improved only slowly, and in some industrial towns got worse for a time in the early 1800s, even as the economy grew. Life expectancy in big industrial cities like Manchester and Liverpool was well below the national average in the 1840s. The evidence from Parliament has to be read with care too. Sadler's 1832 committee collected testimony to support a cause, and a government commission in 1833 concluded that some of its most dramatic claims were exaggerated, while still agreeing that reform was needed. The factory and mines laws also show how regulation grows: early laws without inspectors failed; laws with professional inspectors, reporting duties and penalties gradually worked. Boiler safety followed a similar path, moving from private inspection associations in Manchester (1854–1855) and Hartford (1866) to engineering codes such as the ASME Boiler Code of 1915 and later government regulation. Finally, the link between British industry and slavery is now an active research field. Scholars debate how much profit from slavery and the Atlantic trade financed British industry, but there is no doubt that Lancashire's mills depended on cotton grown by enslaved people for much of the 1800s. About 80 percent of Britain's raw cotton imports in 1860 came from the United States, which is why the American Civil War caused such a severe crisis in Lancashire.
funFact: The wreck of the steamboat Sultana was found in 1982 buried under a soybean field in Arkansas, because the Mississippi River had shifted its course since 1865.
